solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Struggle to keep faith

blocks.note: the surface means an effort or a hard time; the setter means an armed conflict
the surface means to stay loyal; the setter means to defend a religion

explanation.surface: Someone battling to stay loyal through a hard time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep faith' reads as staying loyal or hopeful; taken literally it is a fight to keep a religion, a crusade or jihad.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom taken literally: a crusade or jihad is armed conflict fought to protect a religion.

clue.text: Tough person defending book

blocks.note: hard = tough
in football or rugby a back is a defender

explanation.surface: A hard man standing up for a book under attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person defending' looks like an advocate; it is a sports position, the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A book bound in stiff covers is a hardback.

clue.text: Record of person’s device used by company

blocks.note: a log is a written record
O = of, as in o'clock
a person of a sort, 'an odd type'; the 's is 'has', joining wordplay to definition

explanation.surface: A company keeping a record of a gadget each employee uses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Device' is a gadget in the surface but an emblem in the answer, as in a heraldic device.
explanation.definitionFit: A logotype is a company's emblem or trademark design, its device.

clue.text: Met expectations of what recreates waves

definitions.text: Met expectations of what recreates waves

blocks.note: the surface means hopes were fulfilled; the setter means the predictions of the Met Office
the thing whose wind whips up the sea again and again

explanation.surface: Someone lived up to what people hoped from a thing that makes waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met expectations' reads as 'fulfilled hopes', but Met is the Met Office, Britain's national weather service, and its expectations are a forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Met Office's expected weather, the force that raises waves, is published as a weather forecast.

clue.text: Stand in as secret revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters are overturned into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Someone substituting as an undercover rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand in' reads as one phrase, a deputy; 'Stand' alone is the definition and 'in' starts the fodder. The Resistance was itself a secret revolutionary movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: making a stand against something is opposing it, and that opposition is the noun.

clue.text: Venomous snake — want to catch it

indicators.note: a catcher holds its catch inside

blocks.note: the asp, a small venomous snake
to want is to wish

explanation.surface: A warning about a poisonous snake from someone keen to capture it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Venomous snake' reads as one phrase; 'Venomous' alone is the definition, meaning spiteful, and the snake is the ASP.
explanation.definitionFit: Waspish talk is sharp and spiteful, figuratively venomous.

clue.text: Was unhappy parking in the rain

blocks.note: P = parking, as on road signs
the wet = rainy weather

explanation.surface: A driver was miserable having to park in a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wet' is British for rainy weather, as in 'come in out of the wet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crying is what an unhappy person does, so wept stands for was unhappy.

clue.text: Wallflower has to wither in good shade

blocks.note: to wither is to shrivel, shrink
as written
G = good
violet is a shade of purple

explanation.surface: A wallflower in the garden is fading in a pleasant shady spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all horticulture: wallflower and violet are both plants, and 'shade' looks like shelter from the sun, but it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallflower is a shy person left out at a dance, and a shrinking violet is a timid, retiring person.

clue.text: Native British men in pub

indicators.note: 'in' means inside, so the British men stand inside the pub

blocks.note: B = British
OR = other ranks, ordinary soldiers
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: Locals, British men drinking in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' looks like a noun for the locals; it is the adjective, as in native wit.
explanation.definitionFit: An inborn quality is native to you, present from birth.

clue.text: Well this is rich!

blocks.note: the surface makes it an exclamation; the setter means the word itself, placed in front of the entry
the surface is indignation at cheek; the setter means the two words together mean wealthy

explanation.surface: An exclamation of indignation: well, that's a bit rich!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well, this is rich!' is a cry of outrage at cheek; read literally, 'well' followed by this word makes well-heeled, meaning wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom split in two: well-heeled means wealthy, so this is the half that follows 'well'.

clue.text: Some jazz starts to grow as dance music

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so take G and A

blocks.note: a rag is a piece of ragtime, an early jazz style
first letters of GROW and AS

explanation.surface: Jazz is beginning to evolve into dance music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to grow' reads as 'begins growing'; it asks for the opening letters of 'grow' and 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragga is a Jamaican dance-music style derived from reggae and dancehall.

clue.text: See short story with moral that may be discrete

indicators.note: a short word is cut, so SEE loses its last letter

blocks.note: SEE without its final E
a parable is a simple story teaching a lesson

explanation.surface: A pointer to a brief tale with a lesson that might be kept apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short story' reads as one phrase, but 'short' belongs to 'See'. Discrete (separate) is not discreet (tactful).
explanation.definitionFit: Something that may be discrete, a distinct part, is separable from the rest.

clue.text: Most man-like, except for bust

blocks.note: 'all but one' = all except for one
a bust is the chest

explanation.surface: A statue that looks thoroughly masculine apart from the bust.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets up a woman's figure, so 'bust' seems the odd feature out; it simply gives CHEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Butch means mannish in appearance, so the butchest is the most man-like.

clue.text: Like pork pie, having ground nut and herb

indicators.note: ground nuts are crushed and broken up, so NUT's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: NUT rearranged
rue is a bitter herb

explanation.surface: A pork pie recipe with crushed nuts and herbs.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for lie ('porky'), so something like a pork pie is untrue. 'Ground nut' looks like a peanut.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang: pork pie means lie, and anything like a lie is false.

clue.text: Longing turned into loud cajoling

indicators.note: a thing turned round faces the other way
'into' means entering inside, so the reversed longing goes inside the loud word

blocks.note: a yen is a longing
blaring = very loud

explanation.surface: A quiet yearning turned into noisy coaxing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned into' reads as one phrase, 'became'; here 'turned' reverses the longing and 'into' puts it inside. Blarney is flattering talk, named after the Blarney Stone in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: To blarney is to coax with flattery, so blarneying is cajoling.

clue.text: Lark that is hiding around dicky bird

blocks.note: CA = circa, around
dicky is British slang for unwell or unsound, as in a dicky heart
a lark is a caper, a bit of fun
i.e. = id est, that is

explanation.surface: A lark sheltering beside a poorly little bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Lark and dicky bird both point to birds, but the lark is a prank, CAPER, and dicky means ill. The capercaillie is a large Scottish grouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The capercaillie is a large woodland grouse, a bird.

clue.text: Check delivered sink and shower unit

indicators.note: a speech is delivered out loud

blocks.note: to rein in is to check
to sink is to drop

explanation.surface: A plumber inspecting a newly delivered basin and shower.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is bathroom fittings; 'shower' is weather and a raindrop is one unit of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shower of rain is made of raindrops, each one a unit of the shower.

clue.text: Small talk is hard in peculiar dialect

indicators.note: a peculiar thing is out of the ordinary, so DIALECT's letters take an odd order

blocks.note: H = hard, as on pencils
DIALECT rearranged

explanation.surface: Chit-chat is tricky when the local dialect is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a struggle to converse in an odd accent; 'hard' is only the letter H.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle chat is light, trivial conversation, which is small talk.

clue.text: Harmony daughter found on old lady’s piano

indicators.note: in an across entry one piece on another comes after it

blocks.note: to act in concert is to act in harmony
a gran is a grandmother, an old lady
D = daughter

explanation.surface: A family scene: the daughter discovers grandma's piano and plays in harmony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harmony' suggests music along with the piano, but it gives CONCERT in the sense of agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: A concert grand is the largest size of grand piano, used in concert halls.

clue.text: A duty to convert with Mass in part of temple

indicators.note: converting something changes its form, so A DUTY's letters are changed round

blocks.note: anagram fodder
M = mass, in physics

explanation.surface: A believer's obligation to be converted, with a Mass said in the temple.
explanation.walkthrough: The religious surface makes Mass the church service; here it is the physics symbol M.
explanation.definitionFit: The adytum was the innermost sanctuary of an ancient temple.

clue.text: Fewer clothes, for example

blocks.note: less = fewer
clothes are what you have on

explanation.surface: Wearing fewer clothes, say, in hot weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' reads as a stock phrase; 'example' alone is the definition, in the sense 'let that be an example to you'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson and an example are both warnings to learn from: 'let that be a lesson to you'.

clue.text: The German youth of the 1950s was faster

blocks.note: die is a German word for 'the'
a Teddy boy, the Edwardian-dressed British youth of the 1950s

explanation.surface: A young German in the fifties was quicker than the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faster' reads as quicker; it is someone who fasts, and one who was a faster dieted.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dieted went without food, so was a faster.

clue.text: Faith managed to keep priest in church

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside

blocks.note: Eli, the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible
to run a business is to manage it
CE = Church of England

explanation.surface: A congregation managed to retain its priest.
explanation.walkthrough: Faith, priest and church all suggest religion, but faith here is trust, and the priest is the crossword's regular ELI.
explanation.definitionFit: Reliance is trust or faith placed in someone.

clue.text: Protest over make-up artist?

indicators.note: something turned over faces the other way

blocks.note: to rail against something is to protest

explanation.surface: Complaints about a cosmetics artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up artist' suggests cosmetics; the question mark signals a pun, someone who makes things up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on make-up: someone who makes things up, inventing untruths, is jokingly an artist of it.

clue.text: Conductor to check out in Italy

blocks.note: as written
to scan is to check out
as written
I = Italy, the international vehicle code

explanation.surface: A train conductor checking tickets on a journey through Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' could be on a bus or train; Arturo Toscanini was the great Italian orchestral conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: Toscanini was a famous conductor of orchestras and opera.

clue.text: Ghoulish family member in list

blocks.note: the towering, groaning butler of the Addams Family, the macabre TV and film household
to list is to lean to one side, as a ship does in heavy seas

explanation.surface: A spooky relative appears on a register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'List' reads as a noun, a register; it is the verb, to lean or stagger like a ship, which gives LURCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurch is the Addams Family's butler, and to list is to lurch.

clue.text: Dock with idiot blocking surfer’s view?

indicators.note: a thing blocking a passage sits inside it

blocks.note: a nit is a fool
to moor a boat is to dock it

explanation.surface: A fool is in the way at the harbour, spoiling a surfer's view of the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: The surfer seems to be on a wave, but is surfing the web, and what they look at is a screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A web surfer views pages on a computer monitor.

clue.text: Sink, or attempt to sink?

blocks.note: to decline or be ruined
read as 'go (attempt) to pot (sink a ball)', as in snooker

explanation.surface: A question about whether something sinks or is merely trying to.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is read word by word: a go is an attempt, and to pot is to sink a ball in snooker or pool.
explanation.definitionFit: Going to pot is sinking into decline; having a go at potting is attempting to sink.
